theme: Unit 5 review, The Mosaic Covenant I, Exodus
memoryText: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Exodus 20:2 is the opening line of the Ten Commandments, and it is the unit’s anchor verse. It is easy to skip over it on the way to the commands, but it is the most important sentence in the chapter. Read it aloud once more before you continue.

“I am the LORD your God.” The sentence begins with a name and a relationship. God is the LORD, the covenant God who revealed himself at the burning bush. And he is “your God.” Before there is any command, there is a claim: I belong to you, and you belong to me.

“Who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” This is the basis of the claim. God has already acted. He rescued them when they could not rescue themselves. The authority of the commandments rests on his grace.

“Out of the house of slavery.” It is a wonderful phrase. Egypt was a house, a place of confinement and hard labor, and God brought them out. The rest of the commandments describe what life looks like for people who have been freed. They are no longer slaves, so they do not need to act like slaves, and they are no longer under Pharaoh, so they do not serve other gods.

For the Christian, the verse is a statement about Christ. He is the one who has brought us out of the house of slavery, the slavery to sin and death. “For freedom Christ has set us free” (Galatians 5:1). Obedience is the grateful response of those who have been rescued.
unitRecap:
In Unit 5 you have read the first half of the book of Exodus, from the birth of Moses to the ratification of the covenant at Sinai. You began with Israel in slavery and with Pharaoh’s attempt to destroy the Hebrew sons, and you watched God preserve a baby in a basket. At the burning bush, God revealed his name, I AM WHO I AM, and sent a reluctant Moses to bring his people out. On your first doctrinal day, you studied the existence and attributes of God, from his self-existence to the character of mercy and justice that he proclaimed in Exodus 34.

You followed the confrontation with Pharaoh. The plagues, one after another, were judgments on the gods of Egypt and demonstrations of who the LORD is. You watched Pharaoh bargain and harden his heart. Then came the Passover: a lamb without blemish, its blood on the doorposts, and the promise, “When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” You walked through the Red Sea on dry ground and heard Moses say, “The LORD will fight for you.” You sang the song of Moses and watched the song give way to grumbling at Marah. You prayed through three psalms of the exodus, and saw how the Psalms use the story as a resource for confession, for memory in distress, and for praise.

In the wilderness, God gave manna, water from the rock, and victory over Amalek. At Sinai, God described Israel as a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, and he gave the Ten Commandments, beginning with the words, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out.” On your second doctrinal day, you studied the three uses of the law and how the moral law relates to the Christian. You read the case laws of the Book of the Covenant and saw God’s care for the sojourner, the widow, and the orphan. Finally, you watched the covenant sealed with blood, and the elders eat and drink in the presence of God.

The unit taught that God redeems before he commands, that the blood of the substitute is the ground of safety, and that the exodus is a pattern for all of God’s saving work.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does it matter that God redeems Israel before giving them the law at Sinai?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back at Exodus 19:4 and 20:2. God reminded Israel of what he had done before he told them what to do. How does this order protect us from thinking that we earn salvation by obedience? Write a few sentences about how it changes the way you think about the commands of God in your own life.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the Passover reveal about the nature of atonement?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Think about the lamb without blemish, the blood on the doorposts, and the promise, “When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” What does this teach about substitution and about how God’s judgment and mercy meet? How does it help you understand the death of Jesus?

reviewQuestions.question: What are the three uses of the law, and can you find each one in Exodus?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Recall the civil, the pedagogical, and the normative uses. Where do you see the law restraining a violent people, exposing sin, and guiding the redeemed? Which use do you find most helpful for your own growth, and which do you tend to forget?

reviewQuestions.question: How does the Exodus function as a pattern for all of God’s saving work?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Consider the slavery, the rescue by a mediator, the blood, the passage through water, the covenant, and the journey toward a promised land. Where do you see these themes fulfilled in Christ? Write a short prayer of thanks to Jesus for the greater exodus he has accomplished.

prayerPrompts: Thank God for the exodus and for the greater exodus in Christ.
Ask him to teach you to obey out of gratitude.
Ask him to keep the unit verse near you.
